## Question 1 (5-points)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
students <- data.frame(
  Student = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"),
  Exam_Score = c("85", "92", "78", "NA", "88", "95"),
  Study_Hours = c("5", "8", "3", "6", "NA", "10")
)
```
:::



*The data class of each of these variables is `chr` or character.*


-- Next, write code that would change the variable `Study_Hours` to a numeric variable using `as.numeric()` in a new data set named `s2`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

  mutate(Study_Hours = as.numeric(Study_Hours))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```

Caused by warning:

```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str(s2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
'data.frame':	6 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ Student    : chr  "A" "B" "C" "D" ...
 $ Exam_Score : chr  "85" "92" "78" "NA" ...
 $ Study_Hours: num  5 8 3 6 NA 10
```


:::
:::



-- When you do this, a warning message should be produced. In 2-3 sentences, explain why you are getting this warning message, and what the warning message means. Use the output from `str(s2)` to help answer the question.

The warning is:

```
Caused by warning:
! NAs introduced by coercion 
```

We are getting this warning message because it doesn't know what numeric value NA should take on. So, it strips off the quotation marks, and inputs a missing `NA` value. Changing a character to a missing value that now has a data type of numeric is the definition of coercion.

-- The colors are not colorblind friendly. We can fix this.

```{.r .cell-code}
diamonds |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = carat,
      y = price,
      color = cut
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(

    alpha = .3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Diamonds",
    x = "Carat",
    y = "Price (US dollars)",
```

## Question 4 (5-points)

I am interested in knowing more about the relationship between the cut of the diamond and the price of the diamond. Specifically, I am interested in if we see differences in the price, based on the cut. 

Below, create appropriate summary statistics and an appropriate data visualization to answer the question. Next, in 1-3 sentences, comment on your results. 

*AWV* 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
diamonds |>
  group_by(cut) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(price),
            med = median(price),
            sd = sd(price)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 x 4
  cut        mean   med    sd
  <ord>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Premium   4584. 3185  4349.
2 Fair      4359. 3282  3560.
3 Very Good 3982. 2648  3936.
4 Good      3929. 3050. 3682.
5 Ideal     3458. 1810  3808.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
diamonds |>
  ggplot(
    aes(y = cut, x = price)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](prof_IV_sa_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-8-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


Based on the exploratory data analysis above, we see that premium diamonds have the highest mean value. They also have the highest variability (standard deviation). Surprisingly, we see Fair have the second largest mean, and the lowest standard deviation. Based on our boxplot, and summary statistic, we actually see the Fair cut have the largest median. Ideal cut had the smallest mean and median prices values.
